¶
'''approbative''' (ap′rọ̄-bā-tiv), ''a.'' [= F. ''approbatif'', < L. as if *''approbativus'': see ''approbate'' and ''-ive''.] Approving; expressing, implying, or of the nature of approbation.

'''approbativeness''' (ap′rọ̄-bā-tiv-nes), ''n.'' In ''phren.'', ambition; love of praise or desire for fame; pride of character; sensitiveness to the opinions of others. ''Fowler and Wells.''

'''approbator''' (ap′rọ̄-bā-to̤r), ''n.'' [L., an approver, < ''approbare'', pp. ''approbatus'', approve: see ''approve''<sup>1</sup>.] One who approves formally: as, “judges and ''approbators'',” ''Evelyn'', Letter (1669). [Rare.]

'''approbatory''' (ap′rọ̄-bā-tọ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< ML. ''approbatorius'', < L. ''approbator'': see ''approbator''.] Having the nature of sanction; containing or expressing approbation.
{{smaller block|Letters . . . confirmatory and ''approbatory''.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 457.}}}}

'''approclivity†''' (ap-rọ̄-kliv′i-ti), ''n.'' [< ''ap-''<sup>1</sup> + ''proclivity''.] Proclivity; inclination; tendency.

'''appromt<sup>1</sup>†''' (a-prompt′), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''ad'', to, + ''promptus'', prompt: see ''prompt''.] To prompt; stimulate; encourage: as, “to ''approompt'' our invention,” ''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.

'''approompt<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' [< AF. ''aprompter'', ''apromter'', OF. ''enpromter'', F. ''emprunter'' = Walloon ''epronter'' = It. ''improntare'', borrow, = Wallach. ''inprumutà'', give or take in pledge, < LL. *''inpromutuare'', < ''in promutuum'', in advance (> Wallach. ''inprumùt'', a pledge): L. ''in'', in, for; ''promutuum'', an advance, neut. of ''promutuus'', paid beforehand, advanced, < ''pro'', beforehand, + ''mutuus'', lent: see ''mutual''.] To borrow.

¶ '''approof†''' (a-pröf′), ''n.'' [The mod. form is related to ''approve'' as ''proof'' to ''prove''; ME. ''apprefe'', ''apref'', < OF. ''aprove'', ''apreuve'', proof, trial, < ''aprover'', prove: see ''approve''1, and cf. ''proof''.] '''1.''' The act of proving; trial; test.—'''2.''' Approval or approbation. {{smaller block|He was pleased a marriage feast to crown
With his great presence, and ''approof'' of it. {{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, x. 23.}}}} '''approperate†''' (a-prop′ẹ-rāt), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''approperatus'', pp. of ''approperare'', ''adproperare'', < ''ad'', to, + ''properare'', hasten, < ''properus'', quick, speedy, < ''pro'', forward, + *''-parus'', < ''parare'', make, prepare: see ''pare'', ''prepare''.] To hasten. ''Cockeram''; ''Johnson''. '''appropinquate†''' (ap-rọ̄-ping′kwāt), ''v.'' [< L. ''appropinquatus'', pp. of ''appropinquare'', ''adpropinquare'', < ''ad'', to, + ''propinquare'', bring near, < ''propinquus'', near: see ''propinquity''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To draw near; approach. '''II.''' ''trans.'' To bring near. '''appropinquation†''' (ap″rọ̄-ping-kwā′shọn), ''n.'' [< L. ''appropinquatio(n-)'', < ''appropinquare'': see ''appropinquate''.] '''1.''' The act of coming into near relation or proximity; a drawing nigh. {{smaller block|There are many ways of our ''appropinquation'' to God. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Remains, p. 90.}}}} '''2.''' [Rare.] {{smaller block|The clotted blood within my hose . . . With mortal crisis doth portend My days to ''appropinque'' an end. {{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, I. iii. 590.}}}}

Your own ''appropriaments'', but praising that

readings.c2s3:
¶
'''4.''' In ''law:'' (''a'') The annexing or setting apart of a benefice to the perpetual use of a spiritual corporation. (''b'') The determining to which of several debts a sum of money paid shall be applied. {{smaller|If the debtor does not designate the appropriation, the creditor may; if neither has done so, and litigation arises, the court may do it.—'''Appropriation bill''', a legislative bill proposing appropriations of money for some particular purpose, as for carrying on some department of government.}}

'''appropriative''' (a̤-prō′pri-ā-tiv), ''a.'' [< ''appropriate'' + ''-ive''.] Appropriating; making appropriation; having the power, tendency, or capability of appropriating.

'''appropriator''' (a̤-prō′pri-ā-to̤r), ''n.'' [< LL. as if *''appropriator'', < ''appropriare'', appropriate.] '''1.''' One who appropriates or takes to his own use.
{{smaller block|He knew very well that he was the . . . ''appropriator'' of the money which . . . ought to have fallen to his younger brother.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, xliv.}}}}

'''2.''' In ''eccles. law'', one who is possessed of an appropriated benefice. See ''appropriate'', ''v.'', 4.

'''appropriëtary†''' (ap-rọ̄-prī′e-tā-ri), ''n.'' [Irreg. < ''appropriate'', after ''proprietary''.] Same as ''appropriator'', 2.

'''approvable''' (a̤-prö′va̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''approve''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.] Capable of being approved; meriting approbation.

'''approvableness''' (a̤-prö′va̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' [< ''approvable'' + ''-ness''.] The quality of being approvable.
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''approval''' (a̤-prö′val), ''n.'' [< ''approve''<sup>1</sup> + ''-al.''] The act of approving; approbation; commendation; sanction; ratification.
{{smaller block|A censor . . . without whose ''approval'' no capital sentences are to be executed. {{right|''Sir W. Temple'', Heroic Virtues.}}
He was tender, insinuating, anxious for her ''approval'', eager to unfold himself to her.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Hester, xxii.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Approbation, Approval'' (see ''approbation''), acceptance, consent, authorization.

'''approvance''' (a̤-prö′vans), ''n.'' [< OF. ''aprovance'', < *''aprover'': see ''approve''<sup>1</sup> and ''-ance.''] The act of approving; approbation. [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The people standing all about,
As in ''approvance'', doe thereto applaud.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Epithalamion.}}}}

'''approve'''<sup>1</sup> (a̤-pröv′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''approved'' (rarely pp. ''approven'', after ''proven''), ppr. ''approving''. [Early mod. E. also ''approove'', < ME. ''aproven, appreoven, apreven, appreven'', < OF. ''aprover, approver, approuvir, appreuver, approber'', etc., F. ''approuver'' = Pr. Sp. ''aprobar'' = Pg. ''approvar'' = It. ''approvare'', < L. ''approbare, adprobare'', assent to as good, approve, also show to be good, confirm, < ''ad'', to, + ''probare'', < ''probus'', good: see ''prove.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make good; show to be real or true; prove; confirm; attest; corroborate.
{{smaller block|<poem>What damned error but some sober brow
Will bless it, and ''approve'' it with a text?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 2.}}
<poem>Wouldst thou ''approve'' thy constancy? ''Approve''
First thy obedience. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 367.}}</poem>

To make good; show to be real or true; prove; confirm; attest; corroborate. {{smaller block|What damned error but some sober brow Will bless it, and ''approve'' it with a text? {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Wouldst thou ''approve'' thy constancy? ''Approve'' First thy obedience. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 367.}} The Guardian Angels of Paradise are described as returning to Heaven upon the Fall of Man, in order to ap''prove'' their Vigilance.{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 357.}}}} '''2.''' To show; prove to be; demonstrate. {{smaller block|In all things ye have ''approved'' yourselves to be clear in this matter.{{right|2 Cor. vii. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|’Tis an old lesson; Time ''approves'' it true.{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, ii. 35.}}}} '''3.''' To sanction officially; ratify authoritatively: as, the decision of the court martial was ''approved''. {{smaller block|And by thy coming certainly ''approve'' The pledge of peace. ''Ford'', Honour Triumphant.}} '''4.''' To pronounce good; think or judge well of; admit the propriety or excellence of; be pleased with; commend: as, on trial the goods were ''approved;'' to ''approve'' the policy of the administration. {{smaller block|Yet their posterity ''approve'' their sayings.{{right|Ps. xlix. 13.}}}} {{smaller block|The deed which closed the mortal course of these sovereigns, I shall neither ''approve'' nor condemn.{{right|''Jefferson'', Autobiog., p. 82.}}}} {{smaller block|She wore the colours I ''approved''.{{right|''Tennyson'', The Letters.}}}} '''5.''' To manifest as worthy of approval; commend: used reflexively. {{smaller block|The miracles of Christianity, so far from shocking me, ''approve'' themselves at once to my intellect and my heart.{{right|''Channing'', Perfect Life, p. 248.}}}} '''6.''' To put to the test; prove by trial; try. {{smaller block|Nay, task me to my word; ''approve'' me, lord.{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|A hundred knights with Palamon there came, ''Approv’d'' in fight, and men of mighty name.{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 1299.}}}} Hence—'''7†.''' To convict upon trial or by proof. {{smaller block|He that is ''approv’d'' in this offence. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller|'''Approved bill''' or '''note''', in ''com.'', a bill or note drawn by a solvent, trustworthy party, and to which therefore no reasonable objection can be made.}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To show itself to be; prove or turn out.—'''2.''' To think or judge well or favorably; be pleased: usually with ''of''. {{smaller block|I showed you a piece of black and white stuff, just sent from the dyer; which you were pleased to ''approve of'' and be my customer for. {{right|''Swift.''}}}} '''approve2''' (a̤-pröv′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''approved'', ppr. ''approving''.   [The form ''approve'' (NL. ''approbare, approvare''), confused with ''approve''1, is a mod. error, due to a misunderstanding of the earlier forms; prop. ''approw'', < late ME. ''approwe, aprowe, aproue'', < OF. ''aproer, approer, approuer, apprower'' (> ML. ''approare, appruare'', and later ''appruvare, approvare'', as above), profit, benefit, improve, < ''a'' (L. ''ad''), to, + ''pro, pru, prou, preu'', earliest form ''prod'' (> ME. ''prow''), benefit, advantage, profit: see ''prow''1 and ''prowess''. By a change of prefix, ''approve''2 has become ''improve'', q. v. Cf. ''appair, impair''.]   In ''law'', to turn to one’s own profit; augment the value or profits of, as of waste land, by inclosing and cultivating; improve. {{smaller block|As long ago as the thirteenth century the statute of Merton had authorized the lords of manors to ''approve'', that is, inclose for their own profit, as much of the waste land as would leave enough uninclosed for the use of the commoners. {{right|''F. Pollock'', Land Laws, p. 173.}}}}
